dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe someone who is smart or clever.
examples: That kid is akamai!

dictionary_entries.usage: The ultimate Hawaiian word, representing greetings, farewells, and love.
examples: Aloha, how stay you?

dictionary_entries.usage: The standard local greeting.
examples: Howzit, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe something that is completed.
examples: I pau work.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe a large quantity of something.
examples: Get choke waves today!

dictionary_entries.usage: Expression of gratitude.
examples: Mahalo for the grinds!

dictionary_entries.usage: Reassurance, similar to no problem.
examples: No worry, I got you.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local term for food or eating.
examples: We go get some grindz.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe delicious food.
examples: The poke is real ono!

dictionary_entries.usage: Used for food that is exceptionally delicious.
examples: That kalua pig broke da mouth!

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual address for a male friend or acquaintance.
examples: Eh brah, what's up?

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual address for a female friend.
examples: Howzit, sistah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Term of endearment for a close friend.
examples: Shoots cuz!

dictionary_entries.usage: Formal local spelling of brother/friend.
examples: Eh bruddah, you ready?

dictionary_entries.usage: Verb meaning to be or exist in a state.
examples: I stay hungry.

dictionary_entries.usage: Placed before verbs to indicate past tense.
examples: I wen go beach.

dictionary_entries.usage: Placed before verbs to indicate future tense.
examples: I going surf tomorrow.

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates inability to do something.
examples: I no can go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to express desire.
examples: You like go beach?

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates necessity.
examples: I gotta go home.

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates past negative action (did not).
examples: I neva go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describing wild or crazy behavior.
examples: You stay pupule!

dictionary_entries.usage: Local footwear.
examples: Don't forget your slippahs.

dictionary_entries.usage: Term for grandfather.
examples: I go fish with tutu kane.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to the time after work or happy hour.
examples: We go get drinks for pau hana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Expresses agreement or confirmation.
examples: Shoots, see you later!

dictionary_entries.usage: A teacher or guide.
examples: The kumu says to study.

dictionary_entries.usage: Children or child.
examples: The keiki stay playing.

dictionary_entries.usage: Family, including extended family and friends.
examples: We stay ohana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes something that is a waste or being out of luck / exhausted.
examples: I all poho.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to request a repetition of an action or performance.
examples: Hana hou, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: To eat or get food; also used to describe working hard.
examples: We go grind.
Time for grind.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to childhood days (literally snotty nose days).
examples: Since hanabada days.

dictionary_entries.usage: Means 'later' or 'eventually,' often implying a consequence or result.
examples: Bumbai you learn.
Bumbai we go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Spiritual energy or power.
examples: The place get choke mana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Ghost or supernatural creature.
examples: Spooky obake stories.

dictionary_entries.usage: A visitor or newcomer to the islands.
examples: She one malihini.

dictionary_entries.usage: The land or earth.
examples: Respect the aina.

dictionary_entries.usage: The ocean or sea.
examples: Go makai to the kai.

dictionary_entries.usage: Mountain.
examples: The mauna is covered in snow.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to something being entirely finished.
examples: The food is all pau.

dictionary_entries.usage: To be angry or mad.
examples: Don't get huhu.

dictionary_entries.usage: Mischievous or rascal behavior.
examples: That kid is kolohe.

dictionary_entries.usage: Man or male.
examples: He is one kane.

dictionary_entries.usage: An elder or grandparent.
examples: Listen to the kupuna.

dictionary_entries.usage: To do again, or shout for an encore.
examples: Hana hou! Sing one more!

dictionary_entries.usage: To eat or have food.
examples: We go grind.

dictionary_entries.usage: Nasal mucus, commonly used for runny nose in childhood ('hanabada days').
examples: He got hanabada on his face.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used by surfers to describe large, powerful, hollow, or intimidating waves.
examples: Watch out on da outside, da heavies stay rolling in.
Dat north swell brought da heavies today.

dictionary_entries.usage: Being deep inside the hollow curve of a breaking wave or right in the heaviest spot of the impact zone.
examples: He wen drop in right in da pit!
If you stay in da pit, you gotta hold your breath.

dictionary_entries.usage: Poor, blown-out, choppy, or unrideable wave conditions.
examples: Too much wind today, only get junk surf.
No even bother paddle out, stay junk surf.

dictionary_entries.usage: To surf or skate with high performance, throwing heavy carves and turns.
examples: Look at dat grom shred da gnar at Bowls!
We wen shred da gnar all morning.

dictionary_entries.usage: A surf spot where waves peel along a point of land or reef headland.
examples: Dat spot is one classic point break.
Da point break stay firing on dis south swell.

dictionary_entries.usage: Checking the surf or paddling out at the crack of dawn before crowds arrive.
examples: We go dawn patrol tomorrow at 5:30 AM.
Dawn patrol caught da best sets of da day.

dictionary_entries.usage: When a wave crests and breaks entirely at one time across the reef with no open shoulder to ride.
examples: Every wave was one close out, couldn't make da shoulder.
Watch out fo' dat close out on da inside.

dictionary_entries.usage: Major surf etiquette violation where a surfer takes off on a wave in front of someone who already has right of way.
examples: No drop in on da uncles, brah!
He wen drop in on me and lost his board.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian-style char siu pork bun, available steamed (traditional white) or baked, sold in local shops and manapua trucks.
examples: Pick up one box of steamed manapua from Chinatown.
Da baked manapua stay piping hot!

english: rice topped with burger, egg and brown gravy
dictionary_entries.usage: Iconic Hawaii comfort dish: a bed of white rice topped with a hamburger patty, fried egg, and rich brown gravy.
examples: Gimme one loco moco with two eggs sunny side up.
After surfing, nothing beat one heavy loco moco.

english: seasoned raw fish bowl over rice
dictionary_entries.usage: Fresh cubed ahi or salmon seasoned with shoyu, sesame oil, and scallions served over warm sushi or white rice.
examples: I going buy one spicy ahi poke bowl fo' lunch.
Dat poke bowl had limu and inamona inside.

dictionary_entries.usage: Having an abundant, delicious spread of local food.
examples: Aunty wen cook choke grindz fo' da graduation party.
Get choke grindz at da potluck, come through!

dictionary_entries.usage: Pidgin slang for food or the act of eating.
examples: Time for kau kau, grab one plate!
You like go kau kau after work?

dictionary_entries.usage: Sweet, sour, and salty dried plum powder used to season gummy candies, fresh fruit (like pineapple and apples), or shave ice.
examples: Sprinkle li hing mui on top da gummy bears.
I like my pineapple with choke li hing mui.

english: grilled spam and rice wrapped in seaweed
dictionary_entries.usage: A staple local Hawaii snack consisting of a block of sushi rice topped with glazed grilled Spam and bound with nori.
examples: Grab two spam musubi from 7-Eleven fo' da beach trip.
Spam musubi is da best pau hana snack.

english: local meat entrée with two scoops rice and macaroni salad
dictionary_entries.usage: The quintessential Hawaii meal consisting of two scoops of white rice, one scoop of macaroni salad, and an entrée meat.
examples: We go drive-in get one chicken katsu plate lunch.
No plate lunch complete without mac salad.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Portuguese yeast doughnut fried until golden, coated in granulated sugar or cinnamon, and optionally filled with haupia or custard.
examples: We stopped at Leonard's Bakery fo' hot malasadas.
Da haupia malasadas stay broke da mouth!

dictionary_entries.usage: Finely shaved ice (not crushed) soaked in tropical flavored syrups, often served over vanilla ice cream with azuki beans and sweetened condensed milk (snow cap).
examples: Hot day like today, time fo' rainbow shave ice with snow cap.
Get da best shave ice on North Shore.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional Hawaiian salted, seasoned, and sun-dried beef, often pan-fried before serving.
examples: Dat luau had ono pipikaula and poi.
Pipikaula with hot rice is the best combination.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional Hawaiian coconut milk pudding, sliced into blocks or used as dessert pie/cake filling.
examples: Haupia pie is my favorite dessert at Thanksgiving.
Save some haupia for Uncle.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian word meaning to slice or cut crosswise into pieces; refers to seasoned diced raw fish (usually yellowfin ahi).
examples: Go buy two pounds shoyu poke for the family.
Fresh caught ahi makes the best poke.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes something physically damaged, a person who is exhausted/beaten up, or people laughing uncontrollably.
examples: His truck was all buss up after the trail.
He told one joke and everybody wen buss up laughing.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes someone who is being fake, disingenuous, or putting on a front.
examples: No act all fakafied, just be yourself.
I can tell when someone stay fakafied.

dictionary_entries.usage: A compliment praising someone for being dependable, true to their word, or doing a great favor.
examples: Thanks for picking me up at the airport, you solid bro.
He always shows up when you need help, solid bro.

dictionary_entries.usage: Exclamation when someone looks extraordinarily fly, does a slick maneuver, or is showing off stylish flair.
examples: Check out his custom rims, too much style!
She caught that wave with too much style.

dictionary_entries.usage: Slang contraction of 'guaranteed'; means something is certain or promised.
examples: Guans we going catch fish today.
You coming tonight? Guans, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Admonition telling someone not to act arrogant, show off in public, or make a fool of themselves.
examples: Just stay cool, no make body in front of everybody.
He started yelling, and his friend said 'no make body, brah.'

dictionary_entries.usage: Giving someone a dirty look or glaring with disapproval or irritation.
examples: Why dat guy giving us stink eye?
My mom gave me stink eye when I didn't take off my shoes.

dictionary_entries.usage: Getting goosebumps from emotional music, spooky ghost stories, or awe-inspiring moments.
examples: Hearing that Hawaiian chant gave me pure chicken skin.
Dat haunted road in Pali gives everybody chicken skin.

english: if it's possible, we'll do it; if not, no worries
dictionary_entries.usage: Philosophical local phrase representing a relaxed, flexible attitude toward life and plans.
examples: You think we can finish today? If can, can; if no can, no can!
Just do your best, if can, can.

dictionary_entries.usage: To speak negatively, gossip maliciously, or badmouth people behind their backs.
examples: No talk stink about your cousins.
She always talking stink about her coworkers.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes someone who is sulking, grumpy, or throwing a silent tantrum because they didn't get their way.
examples: Why you stay all habut? It was just a game.
He got habut and walked home by himself.

english: go for a leisure drive or stroll
dictionary_entries.usage: To go out exploring, driving, strolling, or visiting friends with no strict agenda.
examples: Sunday morning we go holoholo on the East Side.
Uncle went holoholo down to the harbor.

dictionary_entries.usage: Enthusiastic contraction of 'all right' used to express agreement, celebration, or excitement.
examples: Aurite! We going beach!
You got the job? Aurite!

english: go for it with full energy
dictionary_entries.usage: Encouragement telling someone to go hard, give full effort, or strike with intensity.
examples: Gee vum, brah! You can score the touchdown!
Time to study for finals, gee vum!

english: getting completely defeated in a game
dictionary_entries.usage: Can refer to a short buzz haircut, or figuratively to being soundly defeated without scoring a point.
examples: He got one fresh shave head for summer.
We got shave head in volleyball today, 21-0.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local pronunciation of 'roger that' meaning affirmative, acknowledged, or agreed.
examples: Meet at 6 PM? Rajah dat!
Rajah dat, I'll bring the cooler.

dictionary_entries.usage: An outdoor porch, covered patio, or open-air veranda on a home or condo.
examples: Let's sit out on the lanai and drink coffee.
The apartment has a huge lanai with ocean views.

dictionary_entries.usage: Cardinal direction in Hawaii meaning toward the mountains or inland (opposite of makai).
examples: Turn mauka at the next intersection.
The mauka side of the highway is clear.

dictionary_entries.usage: Cardinal direction in Hawaii meaning toward the ocean or sea (opposite of mauka).
examples: The park is on the makai side of the street.
Walk makai until you reach the shoreline.

english: local rice dish with hamburger patty, egg, and gravy
dictionary_entries.usage: A staple Hawaii diner comfort dish composed of a bowl of hot white rice topped with a hamburger patty, a sunny-side-up fried egg, and rich brown gravy.
examples: Ho, I stay starving, we go get one loco moco from da diner.
Two scoop rice and extra gravy on top da loco moco.

english: salted salmon side dish with tomatoes and onions
dictionary_entries.usage: A classic Hawaiian side dish made with diced salted salmon, ripe crushed tomatoes, sweet Maui onions, and crushed ice.
examples: No forget da lomi salmon for da luau plate.
Lomi salmon taste so ono wit poi and kalua pork.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian (lomi = massage or mix by hand)

english: octopus or squid simmered in taro leaves and coconut milk
dictionary_entries.usage: A cherished traditional Hawaiian stew prepared by slow-cooking tender octopus or squid with young luau (taro) leaves, coconut milk, and sea salt.
examples: My tutu make da best squid luau on da island.
Squid luau stay rich and sweet from da coconut milk.

dictionary_entries.usage: A chewy, sweet, glutinous rice cake that is a beloved dessert across Hawaii, appearing in variations like butter mochi, chi chi dango, and strawberry mochi.
examples: Aunty brought fresh butter mochi to da potluck.
Dis strawberry mochi stay broke da mouth.

dictionary_entries.usage: A friendly local slang term for a mixed-breed dog, or affectionately for someone of mixed heritage / multicultural background.
examples: My dog is one rescue poi dog, smart as anything.
He got one loyal poi dog dat follow him everywhere.

dictionary_entries.usage: A large platter of mixed appetizers and finger foods served at parties, pau hana gatherings, and local diners.
examples: Order da pupu platter while we wait for da main food.
Da pupu platter get lumpia, chicken wings, and edamame.

dictionary_entries.usage: The essential Pidgin comparative meaning 'much better', 'superior', or 'way more enjoyable'.
examples: Going early morning is mo bettah, no get traffic.
Homemade poke stay mo bettah than store-bought.

dictionary_entries.usage: A common loan phrase used in Hawaii conversation to tell someone to pause, slow down, or wait a second.
examples: Chotto matte brah, I still tying my shoes.
Chotto matte, lemme check da directions first.

english: Puerto Rican dance music in Hawaii
dictionary_entries.usage: A lively genre of Puerto Rican dance music created by immigrants to Hawaii plantations, characterized by accordion, cuatro, and guiro rhythm.
examples: Dey playing kachi kachi music at da graduation party!
Everyone was dancing to da kachi kachi band.
dictionary_entries.origin: Puerto Rican plantation culture in Hawaii

dictionary_entries.usage: Originally sugarcane fiber waste; colloquially used in local plantation slang as a playful or biting term for a rascal or good-for-nothing.
examples: Dat guy acting like real bagasu.
Clean up all dat bagasu from da yard.

dictionary_entries.usage: A button on clothing, or a button on an electronic switch/device.
examples: Push da botan for open da gate.
Your shirt missing one botan, brah.

dictionary_entries.usage: Plantation-era slang word for breaking wind or flatulence.
examples: Who wen make totus in da car?!
Crack da window, someone wen make totus.

english: do not make a fool of yourself
dictionary_entries.usage: Admonition instructing someone to behave with common sense and stop acting crazy or stupid.
examples: Behave in front da kumu, no make lolo.
No make lolo on camera, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Severe highway or island road congestion where cars are packed tightly bumper-to-bumper.
examples: H-1 get choke traffic right now, take da back road.
We was late because had choke traffic going town-bound.

dictionary_entries.usage: A traditional beach necklace or jewelry item made from the worn, naturally holed tip of cone shells found along Hawaiian shorelines.
examples: He wearing his vintage puka shell necklace.
We went hunting for puka shells along da shoreline.

english: island greeting accompanied by shaka sign
dictionary_entries.usage: The quintessential friendly Hawaii greeting and hand gesture expressing goodwill, friendliness, and solidarity.
examples: Shaka brah, good for see you!
Threw him one big shaka brah when he let us merge.

dictionary_entries.usage: Heart, feelings, affection, or moral character. Commonly used in Hawaiian and local expressions of sincerity, aloha, and heartfelt emotion.
examples: From da bottom of my puʻuwai, mahalo nui loa.
Uncle get one big puʻuwai, always taking care da family.
Listen to your puʻuwai when you need for choose da right path.

dictionary_entries.usage: As an adjective, stink describes a bad attitude, not a bad smell: someone acting stink is being mean or rude. It also shows up in stink face (a scowl), alongside stink eye and talk stink.
examples: How come you acting so stink to me?
No be stink, share da musubi wit your sistah.
He get one stink attitude today, no talk to him.
dictionary_entries.origin: From English 'stink', extended in Pidgin from a bad smell to a bad attitude.

english: pork slow-cooked in an underground oven
dictionary_entries.usage: A whole pig cooked in an imu (underground oven) until smoky and tender, then shredded; a lūʻau staple. At home and in plate lunches it is usually made in an oven or slow cooker with Hawaiian salt. Also called kalua pork.
examples: Get kalua pig and cabbage at da plate lunch place.
Uncle wen dig da imu fo' da kalua pig.
Fo' da baby lūʻau get kalua pig, lomi salmon, and poi.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian kālua, to bake in an imu (underground oven).

dictionary_entries.usage: A Pidgin way to say thanks a lot: Hawaiian mahalo plus English plenty (a lot). More casual than mahalo nui loa.
examples: Mahalo plenty fo' da ride, cuz!
Aunty, mahalo plenty fo' da food.
Mahalo plenty, brah, you saved me.

dictionary_entries.usage: Pidgin pronunciation of 'better': the final -er becomes -ah, as in braddah and sistah. At the start of a sentence it means 'you had better' (Bettah you go now). Best known in mo' bettah.
examples: Bettah you go now before da traffic.
Dis one bettah, try taste.
You feeling bettah today?

dictionary_entries.usage: Teasing description of thick, sturdy legs, likened to a daikon radish. Playful between friends, but it is a jab about someone's body, so know your audience.
examples: Ho, dat soccer player get daikon legs, strong!
She wen tease me 'cause I get daikon legs.
All da hiking wen give me daikon legs.
dictionary_entries.origin: From Japanese daikon-ashi (radish legs), brought by Japanese immigrants to Hawaii.

dictionary_entries.usage: Famous island phrase and motto celebrating Maui island pride: 'Maui is the best' or 'Maui is top of the line'. Frequently seen on island bumper stickers, shirts, and signs.
examples: No matta where you go, Maui no ka oi, brah.
Ho, dat sunset from Haleakala proves Maui no ka oi.
Chee-hoo! Maui no ka oi all day!

dictionary_entries.usage: Island Pidgin expression meaning to keep something confidential, secret, or discreet ('on the down-low'). Used when telling someone not to broadcast sensitive news or gossip.
examples: Keep dis news on da lo lo yo, no tell nobody yet.
We stay planning one surprise party, so stay on da lo lo yo.
Brah, dat deal went down on da lo lo yo.
dictionary_entries.origin: Blend of English 'on the down-low' / 'low-low' with Pidgin rhythm and rhyming marker 'yo'.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional and formal Hawaiian letter or email sign-off meaning 'with gratitude' or 'with thanks'. Commonly seen as a closing valediction in local correspondence, formal messages, and community announcements.
examples: Me ka mahalo for your kokua and support.
He wen sign da letter 'Me ka mahalo, Uncle Kimo.'
Me ka mahalo nui loa to all our volunteers today.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Hawaii Chinese-local dim sum classic (siu mai) featuring seasoned ground pork, water chestnuts, and shrimp steamed in an open wonton wrapper.
examples: Grab two manapua and tree pork hash from da bakery.
Dip da pork hash in hot mustard and shoyu, so ono!
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaii Chinese-plantation culinary adaptation of Cantonese siu mai (烧卖).

dictionary_entries.usage: The classic Hawaii local milestone question and phrase describing graduating from school, especially high school, which serves as a core local connection in Hawaii.
examples: What year you went grad?
We wen grad together from McKinley.
His keiki wen grad college on da mainland.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin past-tense preverbal marker 'wen/went' + English 'grad' (graduate).

dictionary_entries.usage: A traditional calming beverage prepared from the roots of the kava plant (Piper methysticum), shared across the Pacific and Hawaii during ceremonies and community gatherings.
examples: Come join da kava circle tonight and talk story.
Drinking kava helps you relax and pau hana in peace.

dictionary_entries.usage: The ancient Hawaiian harvest festival and new year season dedicated to Lono, god of agriculture and fertility, marked by games, sports, feasts, and peace.
examples: During Makahiki season, warfare was forbidden across da islands.
Hauʻoli Makahiki Hou means Happy New Year!

dictionary_entries.usage: The legendary watermen and surf instructors of Waikiki who helped popularize surfing worldwide while serving as ambassadors of aloha.
examples: Uncle was one Waikiki beach boy from small kid time.
Da beach boys know how fo read every single wave.

dictionary_entries.usage: An elegant, formal, floor-length Hawaiian gown with a train, adapted in the 19th century from missionary dresses into a dignified symbol of Hawaiian royalty and modern formal attire.
examples: Tutu wore her velvet holokū for da May Day pageant.
Da singer looked stunning in her silk holokū.

dictionary_entries.usage: Everyday colloquial phrase indicating immediate agreement and that no further explanation or convincing is necessary.
examples: Free food and live music? Nuff said, I stay dea!
Nuff said brah, pack your gear and we go.

dictionary_entries.usage: A casual Pidgin farewell and parting expression meaning 'alright then' or 'see you then'.
examples: Shoots, I see you tomorrow, jah den!
Jah den brah, take care!
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin contraction of 'just then' or 'alright then'.

dictionary_entries.usage: Plantation-era island exclamation expressing disbelief, shock, surprise, or distress.
examples: Ay koodish! How come da tyre stay flat?
Ay koodish, look at da long line!

dictionary_entries.usage: Local slang describing someone with wide, bulging, tired, or blankly staring eyes, resembling an aku (skipjack tuna). Similar to menpachi eyes.
examples: Why you got aku eye like dat? You nevah sleep last night?
He stayed looking at da waves wit aku eye.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local Pidgin term referring to a Catholic priest, pastor, or clerical father figure.
examples: Fadah man wen give da blessing befo' we eat.
Uncle went talk story wit da fadah man aftah church.

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual island hand greeting incorporating a slap, slide, or fist bump between friends and braddahs.
examples: Give da boy dap when you see him.
Shoots brah, throw me one dap.
dictionary_entries.origin: Colloquial greeting gesture adopted widely in island culture.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian Pidgin phonetic pronunciation and spelling of special. Widely recognized in Hawaii literature and everyday speech.
examples: Dis one stay real spesho to me.
Da Good An Spesho Book stay da Pidgin Old Testament.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin phonetic pronunciation of English special.

dictionary_entries.usage: Everyday Pidgin term for vomiting or throwing up. Follows the standard Pidgin th-stopping ("th" -> "t").
examples: Too much malasada, now I feel like I going trow up.
Dat boat ride was rough, almost everyone wen trow up.
dictionary_entries.origin: Pidgin phonology for English throw up.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Samoan term widely embraced across Hawaii meaning brother or close friend, used similarly to brah or bro.
examples: Cheee, what's up uso!
Dat guy my uso from way back, we grew up together.
dictionary_entries.origin: Samoan uso (sibling of the same gender). Commonly used in local Hawaii culture.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe someone who acts entitled, fussy, or demanding like a spoiled child. Commonly heard as "spoil brat".
examples: No be so spoil, eat what stay on your plate.
Dat kid stay one spoil brat when he no get his way.
dictionary_entries.origin: English spoiled, adapted with characteristic Pidgin consonant cluster reduction.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used in local Pidgin to tease someone who is being overly flirty, boy-crazy, or acting coquettish. Often said as gentle teasing among friends and family.
examples: Eh, no be so garut! You just met da guy five minutes ago.
She stay acting all garut in front of da boys.
dictionary_entries.origin: Ilocano garut (flirtatious, promiscuous, or playful). Brought to Hawaii plantations by Filipino laborers and widely adopted into local Pidgin.

examples: I bin go already
I bin go da beach yesterday.
She bin tell me already.
dictionary_entries.usage: This word is used as a past tense marker, similar to 'was' or 'were' in English. It's placed before the verb to indicate that an action happened in the past.
dictionary_entries.origin: The word 'bin' comes from English and is a simplified form of 'been,' used to denote past actions.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: I bin go da beach yesterday.

examples: Ho nah!
Ho nah, you wen' win da lottery?
Ho nah, I can't believe dat!
dictionary_entries.usage: Expresses a heightened level of surprise or disbelief. It's a more emphatic version of 'ho'.
dictionary_entries.origin: A combination of 'ho' with 'nah' (a particle of emphasis), intensifying the expression of surprise.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Ho nah, you wen' win da lottery?

examples: Eh braddah
Eh, braddah, you goin' surf dis weekend?
My braddah from anoda muddah, always got my back.
Wassup bruddah!
Tanks bruddah
dictionary_entries.usage: A term of endearment and camaraderie used between males. It signifies a close friendship or a sense of brotherhood.
dictionary_entries.origin: Derived from the English word "brother," it reflects the close-knit community and the importance of relationships in Hawaiian culture.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, braddah, you goin' surf dis weekend?

examples: Ho, dat wave was huge!
Ho! Dat sunset so beautiful, yeah?
Ho, I neva see nottin' like dat!
dictionary_entries.usage: An exclamation of surprise, amazement, or excitement. It's a versatile interjection used in various situations.
dictionary_entries.origin: This is a Pidgin adaptation of a general exclamation, used to express strong emotion in a concise way.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Ho! Dat sunset so beautiful, yeah?

examples: Let's wala'au story
We stay walaau all night
No walaʻau
dictionary_entries.usage: Having a conversation

examples: Da wahine
She one beautiful wahine.
Da wahine wen' win da race.
dictionary_entries.usage: Wahine means woman or female. It's a respectful term.
dictionary_entries.origin: This is the Hawaiian word for woman.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: She one beautiful wahine.

examples: Das how we do um
Das right, brah!
Das what I mean.
dictionary_entries.usage: A contraction of "that's." It's used to express agreement, confirmation, or to introduce a statement.
dictionary_entries.origin: A simplified contraction of the English phrase "that is," common in casual speech.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Das right, brah!

examples: Da kāne stay working
kane stay man, male, husband
dictionary_entries.usage: Man or husband

examples: Get plenty fish today
You get o wat?
dictionary_entries.usage: Existence or possession
dictionary_entries.audio_example: You get time?

examples: Had plenny people
I had da best shave ice yesterday.
We had fun at da party.
dictionary_entries.usage: This is the past tense form of "to have" or "to be" in Pidgin. It indicates an action or state that occurred in the past.
dictionary_entries.origin: This is a simplified past tense form of the English verb "had," common in Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: I had da best shave ice yesterday.

examples: Dem guys over dea
Dem guys over dere, dey always late.
I saw dem at da store.
dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to them or those people. It's the plural form of "da" or "that."
dictionary_entries.origin: A Pidgin adaptation of the English plural pronoun "them," used to refer to a group of people or things.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Dem guys over dere, dey always late.

examples: Come ova hea
Eh, da plate lunch stay hea, you ready?
Come hea, I gotta tell you somet'ing.
dictionary_entries.usage: Used to indicate the location of something or to call someone's attention. It's a simple and direct way to say 'here'.
dictionary_entries.origin: Derived from the Hawaiian word for 'here', reflecting the importance of place and location in everyday communication.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Come hea, I gotta tell you somet'ing.

examples: I stay tired today
Eh brah, I so tired, I goin' crash early tonight.
After all dat work, da keiki dem stay tired, gotta let dem rest.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, 'tired' reflects a state of fatigue, exhaustion, or sleepiness. It's used in everyday conversation to describe physical or mental weariness, often after a long day or strenuous activity. It can also imply a general lack of energy.
dictionary_entries.origin: The Pidgin word for 'tired' directly reflects the English word, but its usage is deeply embedded in the local culture, reflecting the laid-back lifestyle and the importance of rest and relaxation.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, I so tired, I goin' crash early tonight.

examples: Wat you like eat fo dinnah?
Dis adobo is so sarap!
Eh, dat poke was so sarap, I wen' eat 'em all!
You like try my plate lunch? Da kalua pig so sarap, brah.
dictionary_entries.usage: "Sarap" is used to express enjoyment of food's taste, similar to "delicious" or "tasty." It's often used when describing a particularly good meal or dish, and can be used to describe any food from local plate lunches to international cuisine.
dictionary_entries.origin: Borrowed from Tagalog, "masarap" (delicious) entered Pidgin through Filipino immigrants who came to work on the sugar plantations in the 19th and 20th centuries. It quickly became integrated into the local lexicon.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, dat poke was so sarap, I wen' eat 'em all!

examples: Da ocean stay looking blue today.
Eh, da ocean get big swell today, gotta be careful, brah.
I wen' go swim in da ocean, but da water was too cold, so I just stay on da beach.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Hawaiian Pidgin, 'ocean' can refer to both the nearshore and open sea. It's often used interchangeably with 'kai' (shoreline) and 'moana' (open ocean), depending on the specific context and the speaker's preference. The term is a general descriptor for the body of water surrounding the islands.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term 'ocean' in this context is a direct borrowing from English, reflecting the influence of English on the development of Hawaiian Pidgin. The Pidgin speakers adopted the word to describe the vast body of water surrounding the islands.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, da ocean get big swell today, gotta be careful, brah.

examples: My phone stay dead, no more charge.
Da car battery stay dead, gotta get a jump.
Eh brah, my dog wen' dead las' night, sad, brah.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Hawaiian Pidgin, "dead" (make, pau) is used to describe something that has stopped functioning, like a device with no power, or to express the passing of a person or animal. The term "make" is frequently used before "dead" to emphasize the state of being non-functional or deceased.
dictionary_entries.origin: The Pidgin term "make" likely derives from the English word "make," used to emphasize a state or condition, combined with the English word "dead." This usage reflects the practical and direct nature of Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da car battery stay dead, gotta get a jump.

examples: I love da smell of da sea.
Da sea get real rough today, stay watch out.
We wen go swim in da sea, but da water was too cold.
dictionary_entries.usage: While 'sea' is understood, 'kai' is more commonly used to refer to the ocean in everyday Pidgin. However, 'sea' can be used to emphasize the vastness or wildness of the ocean, especially in descriptions of weather or ocean conditions.
dictionary_entries.origin: The word 'sea' comes from English, reflecting the influence of English speakers on the development of Hawaiian Pidgin. It's usage is less frequent than the Hawaiian word 'kai', which has deeper roots in the local culture.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da sea get real rough today, stay watch out.

examples: Tank you, Aunty
Aunty, you like more poi?
Yeah, Aunty said she goin' bring da malasadas.
dictionary_entries.usage: A term of respect for older women, not necessarily a blood relative. It shows respect and familiarity.
dictionary_entries.origin: This is a cultural practice rooted in the extended family structure of Hawaiian and other Pacific Islander cultures.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Howzit, Aunty?

examples: Everything stay all katsu
Da food stay all katsu, yeah!
We wen' win da game, all katsu!
dictionary_entries.usage: This phrase means everything is perfect, excellent, or victorious. It's used to express satisfaction or approval.
dictionary_entries.origin: This phrase is a Pidgin adaptation, likely influenced by various languages, emphasizing completeness and perfection.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da food stay all katsu, yeah!

examples: 'A'ole, cannot
A'ole, I no like dat
dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian no
dictionary_entries.audio_example: 'A'ole good

examples: My teacher stay giving choke homework.
Da teacher wen tell us no can talk story in class.
Eh, you like go ask da teacher fo' help wit' da problem?
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, 'teacher' can refer to any instructor, but 'kumu' is often preferred, especially for those who teach traditional Hawaiian subjects. The term is used in both formal and informal settings, reflecting the importance of education in the local culture.
dictionary_entries.origin: While 'teacher' is a direct borrowing from English, its usage in Hawaii reflects the historical influence of English-speaking educators and the evolution of Pidgin as a creole language.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da teacher wen tell us no can talk story in class.

examples: Da waves was unreal
Da waves was unreal today!
Dat sunset unreal, brah!
dictionary_entries.usage: Unreal means amazing, awesome, or incredible. It expresses a high degree of positive emotion.
dictionary_entries.origin: This usage is a direct adoption from English slang, but is widely used in Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da waves was unreal today!

examples: Wea you steah?
Da party steah at da beach, yeah?
My car steah broke down, gotta get it tow, brah.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, 'steah' functions as a versatile verb, often replacing 'is', 'are', or 'stays'. It also indicates location or the state of something, reflecting a relaxed and informal communication style.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term 'steah' is a phonetic representation of the English word 'stay' and reflects the influence of English on the development of Hawaiian Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da party steah at da beach, yeah?

examples: He stay hungry mean kine.
Da sun burn mean kine today, gotta stay inside.
She like dat food mean kine, she wen' eat all of it!
dictionary_entries.usage: “Mean kine” is used to emphasize the degree or intensity of something. It's similar to saying “very” or “really,” but with a stronger sense of emphasis and can also express a strong emotion or reaction. It can be used to describe both positive and negative situations.
dictionary_entries.origin: This phrase likely evolved from a combination of English and Hawaiian Creole. The word “mean” is used in its original English sense of “intense” or “significant”, while “kine” is a Pidgin word meaning “kind” or “sort” that is used as a general intensifier.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da sun burn mean kine today, gotta stay inside.

examples: Everyone stay going beach tomorrow.
Everyone get plenny food fo' da potluck, yeah?
Eh, everyone gotta bring dey own towel fo' da beach, okay?
dictionary_entries.usage: In Hawaiian Pidgin, "everyone" (errbody) is used to address a group of people in a casual and inclusive way. It's often used in invitations, announcements, or when giving instructions to a group.
dictionary_entries.origin: The Pidgin term "everyone" reflects the influence of English, but the relaxed and informal usage is characteristic of the local culture.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Everyone get plenny food fo' da potluck, yeah?

examples: Ho, dat one fat fish you caught!
Da plate lunch was so fat, I couldn't even finish 'em!
Eh brah, look at dat fat wave! Perfect fo' surf!
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, "fat" can describe something large or plentiful, but it can also be used to express admiration for something delicious or impressive. It's a versatile word that reflects the Pidgin speaker's appreciation for abundance and quality.
dictionary_entries.origin: The use of "fat" in this context likely evolved from English, but it gained a unique Pidgin flavor through its frequent use in describing food and other desirable things.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, look at dat fat wave! Perfect fo' surf!

examples: I stay nerjis
I get so nerjis fo' da test, I couldn't even tink.
You lookin' real nerjis, you okay?
dictionary_entries.usage: Describes a state of nervousness or anxiety. It's often used before a stressful event or when someone is feeling uneasy.
dictionary_entries.origin: A Pidgin pronunciation of 'nervous,' highlighting the influence of English.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: I get so nerjis.

examples: Go help Tante in da kitchen.
Tante, can you check if da rice is ready?
My tante always makes da best malasadas.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, "tante" is a term of endearment and respect for a woman, often an older relative or family friend. It's used similarly to "aunty" but can carry a slightly different cultural weight, especially in families with European or Filipino heritage. It reflects the close-knit nature of many Hawaiian communities.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term "tante" likely entered Pidgin through contact with European (particularly German) and Filipino communities who used similar terms for aunts or older female relatives. This linguistic blending is common in Hawaiian Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Tante, can you check if da rice is ready?

examples: Stay dea, I going come
Eh brah, you see da car ova dea?
I wen leave um dea las' night, gotta go get um.
dictionary_entries.usage: "Dea" is a versatile Pidgin term, functioning as a demonstrative pronoun and adverb, similar to "there" or "that place" in English. It's used to indicate a specific location or to point out something that's already been mentioned or is within sight.
dictionary_entries.origin: This word evolved from the English phrase "there," and its usage reflects the localized pronunciation and grammatical adaptation common in Hawaiian Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, you see da car ova dea?

examples: I no like dat

dictionary_entries.usage: Article 'the'

examples: You done with your lunch?

dictionary_entries.usage: While 'done' exists in Pidgin, it's less frequent than 'pau'. It's often used for emphasis or to mirror Standard English, especially in questions or when confirming completion. It can also be used to show a more casual or relaxed tone.
dictionary_entries.origin: Borrowed directly from English, 'done' maintains its original meaning in Pidgin but is less prevalent than the native Pidgin term 'pau'.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: You done with da work, yeah?

examples: Dat buggah is crazy
Da buggah stay big
Which buggah you talking about?

dictionary_entries.usage: "Buggah" is a versatile term in Pidgin, often used to refer to a person, but it can also describe a thing or situation. It can express a range of emotions, from affection to frustration, depending on the context and tone of voice.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term "buggah" likely evolved from a combination of English slang and local adaptation, becoming a core part of Pidgin vocabulary to fill a variety of conversational needs.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, dat buggah wen' steal my plate lunch!

examples: You need some help with dat?
Eh brah, can you help me move dis couch?
She always ready to help, yeah? Real good kine person.
dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, 'help' is a common word, but it can also be expressed through actions. It's used in everyday situations, from asking for physical assistance to offering emotional support. The context often reveals the specific type of help needed.
dictionary_entries.origin: Pidgin's 'help' comes from English, reflecting the language's roots in the plantation era, where diverse communities needed a common language for communication and mutual aid.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, can you help me move dis couch?

examples: Negz, cannot

He aks me fo' help, I said negz.
dictionary_entries.usage: A simple and direct way to say 'no' or to express disagreement. It's a quick and common response.
dictionary_entries.origin: A Pidgin simplification of 'negative,' demonstrating the language's efficiency.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Negz, I stay home.

examples: Da party was all nuts last night
Da party stay all nuts las' night.

dictionary_entries.usage: This phrase describes a situation or person that is crazy, wild, or chaotic. It can be used to describe exciting or overwhelming situations.
dictionary_entries.origin: This phrase is a Pidgin adaptation, using the English word 'nuts' to describe a state of craziness.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da party stay all nuts las' night.

examples: No worry, beef curry! We going make 'em on time.
You forgot your wallet? Beef curry no worry brah, I got you.
dictionary_entries.usage: A playful rhyming Pidgin catchphrase used to reassure someone that there is nothing to stress about.

examples: Pass me dat ting over dere on da table.

dictionary_entries.usage: The standard Pidgin pronunciation of 'thing', used to refer to any object, gadget, or topic.

examples: You like eat, eh? I going cook

You like eat, eh? Get choke food
You like eat, eh? I wen' make plate lunch.

dictionary_entries.usage: This phrase is a common way to offer food or inquire if someone is hungry. It's a friendly and casual way to check in with someone, often used when sharing a meal or offering a snack.
dictionary_entries.origin: This Pidgin phrase reflects the importance of food and hospitality in Hawaiian culture, stemming from the diverse immigrant groups who came to the islands and shared meals together.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: You like eat, eh? I wen' make plate lunch.

examples: Da food stay winnahz
Da food was winnahz!
Dis shave ice, winnahz, brah!
dictionary_entries.usage: "Winnahz" means "delicious" or "awesome." It's an enthusiastic expression of approval or enjoyment. It's a positive adjective for something that is really good.
dictionary_entries.origin: This is a Pidgin adaptation of the English word "winners."
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da food was winnahz!

examples: Time fo' gohan!
I go eat gohan now.

dictionary_entries.usage: "Gohan" means "rice" or "meal." It's a common term, especially in the context of plate lunches. It reflects the influence of Japanese culture on Hawaii.
dictionary_entries.origin: This word is borrowed from the Japanese language, reflecting the influence of Japanese immigrants on Hawaiian culture.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: I go eat gohan now.

examples: I go store, you like anything?

dictionary_entries.audio_example: We go!

dictionary_entries.origin: A Pidgin pronunciation of "cherry," used to describe the color red.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da cherreh car, yeah?

dictionary_entries.origin: This is a simplified pronunciation of the English word "this," common in Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Dis is my friend, John.

examples: Ho, brah! You see dat?

dictionary_entries.origin: A quintessential Pidgin phrase, "ho" is a general interjection, and "brah" is a term of camaraderie, reflecting the close-knit community spirit of Hawaii.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Ho, brah

dictionary_entries.audio_example: Dat was off da hook!

examples: I stay hungry brah

dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, 'hungry' is used just like in English, but often with the intensifier 'so' to emphasize the feeling. It's a common expression used in everyday conversations about food and meal times.
dictionary_entries.origin: The Pidgin word 'hungry' comes directly from English, reflecting the influence of the English language on the development of Hawaiian Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, I so hungry, gotta go grab some plate lunch.

dictionary_entries.audio_example: kine

dictionary_entries.origin: This is a simplified pronunciation of the English word "that," common in Pidgin.

examples: Throw away dat boro boro shirt already!

dictionary_entries.usage: "Boro boro" is used to describe something that is worn out, dilapidated, or in a state of disrepair. It can apply to clothing, vehicles, buildings, or any object that has seen better days and is falling apart.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term "boro boro" comes from the Japanese word "boro-boro," meaning "ragged" or "worn out." It was adopted into Pidgin English through the influence of Japanese immigrants who came to Hawai'i to work on the sugar plantations.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da car stay boro boro, gotta get a new one.

dictionary_entries.origin: Deeply rooted in Hawaiian culture, the hula is a sacred dance form that tells stories, preserves history, and honors the gods and goddesses.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: She like learn hula.

dictionary_entries.usage: "Bambucha" is used to describe something of an exceptionally large size, often with a sense of awe or exaggeration. It's a common term in Pidgin, highlighting the speaker's surprise or emphasis on the size of an object or situation.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term "bambucha" is a Pidgin word, likely derived from a combination of influences, including English and possibly other languages spoken by plantation workers. It reflects the expressive and colorful nature of Pidgin.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da wave was bambucha, brah, almost wen' wash 'em all away!

examples: Just minahs

dictionary_entries.usage: In Hawaiian Pidgin, "minahs" signifies something insignificant or trivial. It's often used to downplay a problem or situation, indicating it's not worth significant concern or effort.
dictionary_entries.origin: Derived from the English word "minor," "minahs" reflects the Pidgin language's tendency to adapt and shorten words for everyday use.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Da problem, just minahs, brah.

examples: You mento

dictionary_entries.usage: "Mento" is used to describe someone who is acting irrationally, strangely, or is perceived as mentally unstable. It can also be used playfully among friends to tease someone for doing something silly or unexpected.
dictionary_entries.origin: Derived from the English word "mental," "mento" in Pidgin gained its own unique flavor through local usage and the Pidgin language's tendency to adapt and simplify words.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, you mento fo' real!

dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, "mayjah" is used to emphasize the size, importance, or severity of something. It can describe a significant problem, a large amount, or a serious situation, often intensifying the meaning of the word it modifies.
dictionary_entries.origin: Derived directly from the English word "major," "mayjah" reflects the influence of English on the development of Hawaiian Pidgin. Its adoption highlights the practical need for words to describe importance and scale.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh brah, dat's one mayjah lie you tell!

dictionary_entries.usage: This is the Pidgin form of "going," used to indicate a future action or intention. It's a common way to express plans or arrangements.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes someone who is extremely tired, worn out, or exhausted. It conveys a feeling of being completely drained of energy.
dictionary_entries.origin: This phrase likely evolved from a combination of English and local slang to express the feeling of exhaustion.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: I boro boroz afta dat long hike.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to the lychee fruit, a sweet and juicy tropical fruit. It's a popular treat. It's a fruit.

dictionary_entries.audio_example: Lychee

examples: We going catch i'a today

dictionary_entries.usage: The general term for fish. It's a common term. It's a food source.
dictionary_entries.origin: From the Hawaiian language, reflecting the importance of fishing in Hawaiian culture and diet.

examples: That guy stay solid, you can trust him

examples: All katsu now!

dictionary_entries.usage: Means perfect, victorious, or winning. It expresses complete success or satisfaction.
dictionary_entries.origin: From the Japanese word 'katsu,' meaning victory, reflecting the influence of Japanese culture in Hawaii.

examples: That's one big kine problem

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to emphasize the size, importance, or degree of something. It intensifies the adjective that follows, indicating something is significant or substantial.
dictionary_entries.origin: This phrase is a Pidgin construction, using "big" (large) and "kine" (kind of/type of) to create an intensifier.

dictionary_entries.usage: "Manini" is used to describe something small in size or value, but it can also refer to someone who is stingy or unwilling to share. It's a versatile word that reflects both physical characteristics and personality traits, often used in a casual, everyday context.
dictionary_entries.origin: The term originates from the Hawaiian language, referring to the convict tang fish, which are small in size. Over time, its meaning expanded to encompass other senses of smallness and stinginess.
dictionary_entries.audio_example: Eh, dat kine manini kine car, yeah?

examples: Time fo' kaukau!

dictionary_entries.usage: Means food or a meal, and can also be used as a verb meaning "to eat." It's a general term for nourishment.

examples: Howzit, palala! Long time no see!

examples: Dass correck

dictionary_entries.audio_example: Yeah, brah, you correck!

examples: Lets go jump in the moana to cool off.

dictionary_entries.usage: In Pidgin, "moana" is used to describe the ocean, encompassing both the vast open sea and the waters surrounding the islands. It's a common term in everyday conversation, reflecting the central role the ocean plays in Hawaiian life.
dictionary_entries.origin: The word "moana" comes directly from the Hawaiian language, where it also means "ocean" or "sea." This highlights the strong connection between the people and the ocean.

dictionary_entries.origin: The term "kahiko" is directly from the Hawaiian language, reflecting the importance of the past and the preservation of ancestral knowledge in Hawaiian culture.

dictionary_entries.origin: The term "lolo" comes from the Hawaiian language, where it originally meant "brainless" or "crazy." It has been adopted and adapted within Pidgin to reflect local attitudes and humor.

dictionary_entries.origin: This Pidgin term originates from the Hawaiian language, where "moe" means "to sleep." The repetition, "moe moe," emphasizes the feeling of sleepiness.

stories.title: Shopping at Chinatown Market
stories.pidgin_text: Saturday morning, Mama and little Leilani go Chinatown fo' buy groceries. 'Eh, how much dis dragon fruit?' Mama ask da vendor. 'For you, special price - five dollah!' he say wit' one big smile. Leilani stay looking at all da colorful fruits - lychee, rambutan, star fruit. 'Mama, wot dis red ting?' she ask, pointing at one exotic fruit. 'Dat's dragon fruit, baby. Very sweet inside.' They fill up their bag wit' all kine local produce. 'Dis market get da freshest kine food on da island,' Mama tell her daughter.
stories.english_translation: Saturday morning, Mom and little Leilani go to Chinatown to buy groceries. 'Hey, how much is this dragon fruit?' Mom asks the vendor. 'For you, special price - five dollars!' he says with a big smile. Leilani is looking at all the colorful fruits - lychee, rambutan, star fruit. 'Mom, what is this red thing?' she asks, pointing at an exotic fruit. 'That's dragon fruit, baby. Very sweet inside.' They fill up their bag with all kinds of local produce. 'This market has the freshest kind of food on the island,' Mom tells her daughter.
stories.cultural_notes: Honolulu's Chinatown is a vibrant cultural district where many locals shop for fresh produce, especially Asian fruits and vegetables. The multicultural aspect of Hawaii is reflected in the diverse food offerings.

stories.title: Hula Practice with Kumu
stories.pidgin_text: Every Thursday evening, da hula halau meet at da community center. 'Remember girls, hula is not just dancing,' explain Kumu Leilani. 'Each movement tell one story.' Little Nalani stay struggling wit' da hand motions. 'Eh Nalani, no worry,' her Kumu say gently. 'Just feel da music in your heart.' Da older dancers help da young ones learn da traditional steps. 'When you dance hula, you connecting wit' your ancestors,' Kumu continue. 'Dis is how we keep our culture alive.' By da end of practice, all da wahine feel proud of what they accomplished.
stories.english_translation: Every Thursday evening, the hula school meets at the community center. 'Remember girls, hula is not just dancing,' explains Teacher Leilani. 'Each movement tells a story.' Little Nalani is struggling with the hand motions. 'Hey Nalani, don't worry,' her teacher says gently. 'Just feel the music in your heart.' The older dancers help the young ones learn the traditional steps. 'When you dance hula, you're connecting with your ancestors,' Teacher continues. 'This is how we keep our culture alive.' By the end of practice, all the women feel proud of what they accomplished.
stories.cultural_notes: Hula is the traditional Hawaiian dance that tells stories through graceful movements. A halau is a hula school, and Kumu means teacher. Hula is considered a sacred art form that connects practitioners to Hawaiian culture and spirituality.

stories.title: Aunty Lei's Kitchen
stories.pidgin_text: Every Sunday, all da keiki come ovah Aunty Lei's house fo' grind. She stay cooking dat ono kine food - kalua pig, poi, haupia cake. 'Eh, you guys hungry or what?' she call out. 'Come, come! No be shy!' All da cousins rush inside, da smell stay so good. 'Wot you wen make today, Aunty?' ask little Keoni. 'Same same every week,' she laugh. 'But you nevah get tired, yeah?' Dis da kine tradition dat keep da ohana together.
stories.english_translation: Every Sunday, all the children come over to Aunty Lei's house to eat. She's cooking that delicious kind of food - kalua pig, poi, haupia cake. 'Hey, are you guys hungry or what?' she calls out. 'Come, come! Don't be shy!' All the cousins rush inside, the smell is so good. 'What did you make today, Aunty?' asks little Keoni. 'Same thing every week,' she laughs. 'But you never get tired, right?' This is the kind of tradition that keeps the family together.
stories.cultural_notes: Hawaiian families often gather on Sundays for large meals. Kalua pig is traditional Hawaiian barbecue, poi is a staple made from taro root, and haupia is coconut pudding cake. The concept of 'ohana' (family) extends beyond blood relations.

stories.title: Big Wave Surfing at Pipeline
stories.pidgin_text: Brah, you see dat set coming in? Dose waves stay HUGE! Kawika grab his board real quick. 'Eh, I going charge 'em!' he tell his friends. 'You stay crazy or what?' they say. But Kawika, he one local boy, been surfing Pipeline since small kid time. He paddle out, wait fo' da perfect wave. Boom! One monster wave come. He drop in, ride 'em all da way. 'Ho, dat was sick!' everybody stay cheering from da beach.
stories.english_translation: Bro, do you see that set of waves coming in? Those waves are HUGE! Kawika grabs his board really quickly. 'Hey, I'm going to charge them!' he tells his friends. 'Are you crazy or what?' they say. But Kawika, he's a local boy, has been surfing Pipeline since he was a little kid. He paddles out, waits for the perfect wave. Boom! A monster wave comes. He drops in, rides it all the way. 'Wow, that was amazing!' everyone is cheering from the beach.
stories.cultural_notes: Pipeline on Oahu's North Shore is one of the world's most dangerous and famous surf breaks. Local surfers like Kawika grow up with deep respect for the ocean and often start surfing as young children.

stories.title: Tutu Kane's Fishing Wisdom
stories.pidgin_text: Old Tutu Kane wake up 4 o'clock every morning fo' go fishing. 'Eh grandson,' he tell young Makoa, 'you like come wit' me today?' Makoa stay sleepy but he know dis one special ting. Down at da pier, Tutu Kane teach him how fo' tie da hooks, wot kine bait fo' use. 'Da fish, they smart yeah? You gotta be patient, wait fo' da right moment.' All day they stay quiet, just enjoying da ocean breeze. When they catch one big mahi-mahi, Tutu Kane smile. 'Dis da kine memories dat stay wit' you forever, boy.'
stories.english_translation: Old Grandfather wakes up at 4 o'clock every morning to go fishing. 'Hey grandson,' he tells young Makoa, 'do you want to come with me today?' Makoa is sleepy but he knows this is a special thing. Down at the pier, Grandfather teaches him how to tie the hooks, what kind of bait to use. 'The fish, they're smart you know? You have to be patient, wait for the right moment.' All day they stay quiet, just enjoying the ocean breeze. When they catch a big mahi-mahi, Grandfather smiles. 'These are the kind of memories that stay with you forever, boy.'
stories.cultural_notes: Tutu Kane means grandfather in Hawaiian. Fishing is deeply ingrained in Hawaiian culture, representing both sustenance and spiritual connection to the ocean. The practice of kupuna (elders) teaching keiki (children) traditional skills is central to cultural preservation.

stories.title: First Day on the Job
stories.pidgin_text: Ho brah, my first day work was one trip! Da boss tell me, 'Eh, you da new guy yeah? No worry, we going show you how we do.' I was so nervous, hands stay shaking. But den dis one aunty from accounting come ovah, 'Eh, relax. We all ohana hea. You like some coffee?' She wen bring me one fresh malasada too. By pau hana time, I felt like I been working dea my whole life. Dat's da aloha spirit, brah.
stories.english_translation: Wow man, my first day of work was quite an experience! The boss tells me, 'Hey, you're the new guy right? Don't worry, we're going to show you how we do things.' I was so nervous, my hands were shaking. But then this one lady from accounting came over, 'Hey, relax. We're all family here. Would you like some coffee?' She brought me a fresh malasada too. By the end of work, I felt like I had been working there my whole life. That's the aloha spirit, man.
stories.cultural_notes: Hawaiian workplaces often have a strong sense of 'ohana' (family). Malasadas are Portuguese donuts that are extremely popular in Hawaii. 'Pau hana' refers to the time after work is finished.

stories.title: Fishing with Grandpa
stories.pidgin_text: Every Saturday, me and my tutu kane go down da pier fo' fish. He get his special spot, been going dea since small kid time. 'Eh, you gotta be patient,' he always tell me. 'Da fish going come when dey ready.' We sit dea, talk story about da old days. He tell me about when Haleiwa was all pineapple fields. No cars, no tourists, just da locals. 'Ho, was different time,' he say, looking at da ocean. I love dose days with tutu. Dat's how we pass down da culture, one fishing trip at a time.
stories.english_translation: Every Saturday, my grandfather and I go down to the pier to fish. He has his special spot, been going there since he was a child. 'Hey, you've got to be patient,' he always tells me. 'The fish will come when they're ready.' We sit there, chatting about the old days. He tells me about when Haleiwa was all pineapple fields. No cars, no tourists, just the locals. 'Wow, it was a different time,' he says, looking at the ocean. I love those days with grandpa. That's how we pass down the culture, one fishing trip at a time.
stories.cultural_notes: Fishing is an important cultural activity in Hawaii, passed down through generations. 'Tutu kane' is the Hawaiian term for grandfather.
